strengths: The paper addresses a challenging and practically relevant problem: translating a single exocentric (third-person) image into an egocentric (first-person) view.

The proposed conceptual pipeline—combining geometric unprojection/reprojection via hand pose alignment with multimodal diffusion inpainting conditioned on text, pose, and sparse maps—is an intuitive design.
The qualitative examples and in-the-wild smartphone demonstrations illustrate the visual promise of using sparse geometric maps together with diffusion models.
weaknesses: Critical discrepancy between the paper's core claims and experimental setup: The paper strongly criticizes existing methods for relying on 'unrealistic assumptions such as necessity of initial egocentric frame and relative camera poses during inference.' However, Section 4.3 reveals that on H2O, the method uses 'ground-truth egocentric sparse maps, which are derived directly from the ground-truth exocentric depth maps and relative camera poses.' Furthermore, on TACO, it uses 'both the ground-truth hand poses and egocentric sparse maps.' Consequently, the quantitative results in Table 1 do not evaluate the proposed full pipeline (which predicts depth, egocentric hand pose, and camera transformation), undermining the central claim of camera-pose-free translation.

Missing key state-of-the-art baselines: Although the authors discuss Exo2Ego (ECCV 2024) and 4Diff (ECCV 2024)—methods specifically formulated for exocentric-to-egocentric translation—neither is included in the quantitative benchmark comparisons in Table 1. Instead, the paper only compares against generic or older baselines (pix2pixHD, pixelNeRF, and CFLD), leaving the true competitiveness against existing task-specific methods unverified.

Missing end-to-end quantitative evaluation and error propagation analysis: The paper does not provide quantitative experiments evaluating the performance drop when using the estimated components (predicted depth, predicted 3D egocentric hand pose via the ViT-MLP model, and Umeyama alignment) versus the ground-truth sparse maps. Hand keypoints are local and articulated; estimating rigid 6DoF camera poses purely from predicted hand keypoints via Umeyama is inherently prone to large rotational errors.

Limited applicability on datasets where hands/head are unconstrained: As admitted in the implementation details, the egocentric hand pose estimator is infeasible on TACO due to head motion/occlusion, forcing the authors to provide ground-truth poses. This highlights a significant fragility in the core transformation mechanism.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem in computer vision: translating single-view exocentric observations to an egocentric viewpoint.
The conceptual combination of geometric reprojection (exocentric point cloud lifting and transforming) with diffusion-based inpainting and multimodal conditioning (pose and text) is well-motivated.
The paper includes qualitative demonstrations on in-the-wild smartphone captures to showcase potential real-world utility.
weaknesses: Critical flaw in benchmark evaluation and contradiction of core claims: In Section 4.3, the authors state that on H2O, they use ground-truth egocentric sparse maps derived directly from ground-truth exocentric depth maps and ground-truth relative camera poses, and on TACO, they use ground-truth hand poses and egocentric sparse maps. This directly contradicts the central premise of the paper—that EgoWorld solves exocentric-to-egocentric translation from a single image without requiring known relative camera poses. Because ground-truth geometry is injected during testing, the quantitative benchmark results in Table 1 do not evaluate the proposed single-view pipeline.

Absence of key state-of-the-art baselines: While the paper cites and discusses direct exocentric-to-egocentric translation methods such as Exo2Ego (ECCV 2024) and 4Diff (ECCV 2024), none of these methods are evaluated in the benchmark experiments. Instead, the method is compared only against older/mismatched baselines (pix2pixHD from 2018, pixelNeRF from 2021) and a person image synthesis model (CFLD), which makes the claimed SOTA performance unconvincing.

Lack of quantitative evaluation for Stage 1 components: The intermediate modules responsible for making the method fully automatic—specifically the learned 3D egocentric hand pose estimator, depth metric calibration, and Umeyama-based camera pose estimation—are evaluated only qualitatively (Fig. A). There are no quantitative metrics (such as MPJPE, PA-MPJPE, or rotation/translation errors), nor is there an evaluation comparing full end-to-end inference (estimated sparse maps) against the GT sparse map setting.

Limited technical novelty: The pipeline mostly assembles existing off-the-shelf tools (VGGT for depth, ACR for exocentric hand pose, Qwen-VL for text captioning, Umeyama for rigid alignment) and fine-tunes a standard Latent Diffusion Inpainting model with concatenated feature channels.

Insufficient training details and ablation scope: Training for only 5 epochs with a batch size of 3 on a single GPU suggests very limited training, and all ablation experiments (Tables 2 and 3) are restricted to a single split (unseen objects) without measuring end-to-end degradation when intermediate estimations fail.

strengths: Translating third-person (exocentric) views to first-person (egocentric) views from a single image is a compelling and challenging problem with high relevance to AR/VR and robotics.
The conceptual integration of geometric projection (via depth and 3D hand pose alignment) with diffusion-based inpainting and VLM-based semantic conditioning is intuitive and logically structured.
The qualitative results, including ablation visualizations and in-the-wild smartphone tests, demonstrate reasonable visual quality and coherent completions.
The paper provides ablations comparing different conditioning modalities (text and pose) as well as alternative inpainting backbones (MAE, MAT).
weaknesses: Severe discrepancy between claims and experimental protocol: The paper explicitly criticizes prior work for relying on known relative camera poses during inference. However, Section 4.3 states that on H2O, ground-truth egocentric sparse maps derived directly from ground-truth exocentric depth and relative camera poses are used, and on TACO, both ground-truth hand poses and egocentric sparse maps are used. As a result, the primary quantitative benchmark (Table 1) does not evaluate the proposed camera-free, end-to-end pipeline; the actual performance when using estimated depth, predicted egocentric hand pose, and Umeyama alignment remains unmeasured.

Critical missing baseline: Exo2Ego (Luo et al., ECCV 2024, Ref [13]) is the most direct prior work addressing single-image exocentric-to-egocentric translation, and the authors explicitly adopt the exact benchmark splits from [13]. However, Exo2Ego is completely omitted from the quantitative evaluation in Table 1. Comparing only against general models like pix2pixHD (2018), pixelNeRF (2021), and person-reposing CFLD (2024) is insufficient and misleading.

Unfair baseline comparison: The baselines compared in Table 1 (pix2pixHD, pixelNeRF, CFLD) do not have access to ground-truth projected sparse egocentric maps, giving the proposed method an unfair advantage in the reported metrics.

Limited technical novelty: The pipeline largely consists of an assemblage of existing off-the-shelf foundation models and algorithms (VGGT, ACR, Umeyama algorithm, Qwen-VL, CLIP, and LDM inpainting). The only newly trained observation component—the ViT+MLP egocentric hand pose regressor—is barely analyzed and bypassed in the TACO experiments.

Lack of analysis regarding geometric alignment robustness: Aligning coordinate frames solely via hand keypoints using the Umeyama algorithm is susceptible to noise, keypoint ambiguity, occlusion, and coplanarity issues. The paper does not provide quantitative sensitivity analysis for pose errors or alignment failures.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: translating a single exocentric (third-person) image into an egocentric (first-person) view without requiring pre-calibrated relative camera poses, multiple synchronized viewpoints, or reference first-person frames.

Well-motivated combination of geometric reasoning and generative diffusion: using metric hand depth calibration and 3D hand pose estimation in both coordinate frames to derive the exocentric-to-egocentric rigid transformation via the Umeyama algorithm, effectively framing the translation as multimodal-conditioned inpainting from a reprojected sparse point cloud.
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple diverse benchmarks (H2O, TACO, Assembly101, and Ego-Exo4D) evaluating generalization over unseen objects, actions, scenes, and subjects.

Extensive ablations and analyses, including conditioning modalities, impact of imperfect/noisy textual prompts, robustness under noisy observations, pose modeling variants, and image completion backbones.
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons have certain limitations: key recent domain-specific methods such as Exo2Ego and 4Diff could not be compared directly due to lack of public source code, leading the authors to rely on proxies (CFLD) and internal ablations alongside older general-purpose baselines (pix2pixHD, pixelNeRF).

Reliance on 3D hand keypoints for camera transformation: deriving the full 6DoF rigid transformation solely from hand keypoint correspondence via the Umeyama algorithm is susceptible to errors when hands are partially occluded, fast-moving, or when hand keypoint estimation suffers from depth ambiguity.

Unclear handling of camera intrinsics for in-the-wild inference: the reprojection step requires an egocentric intrinsic matrix $K_{ego}$. The paper does not clearly specify how $K_{ego}$ is selected or assumed when testing on arbitrary in-the-wild smartphone photographs.

Extension to video remains preliminary: while the paper primarily targets image translation, practical applications typically operate on video sequences. The simple latent blending heuristic in Appendix A.2.7 causes a noticeable drop in per-frame quality, leaving full temporal modeling to future work.

strengths: Formulates a practical and challenging setup for single-view exocentric-to-egocentric translation without requiring ground-truth relative camera poses, calibrated multi-view rigs, or prior egocentric reference frames at test time.

Presents an effective hybrid geometric-generative pipeline: leveraging metric hand pose estimation to resolve monocular depth scale ambiguity and using Umeyama alignment between predicted exocentric and egocentric hand poses to derive the cross-view transformation.

Extensive experimental evaluation across four major benchmarks (H2O, TACO, Assembly101, Ego-Exo4D) with comprehensive generalization splits (unseen objects, actions, scenes, subjects) and clear quantitative gains across perceptual and geometric metrics.

Thorough ablation studies and diagnostic analyses, including investigations into conditioning modalities, inpainting backbones, hand pose representations, robustness under noise, and qualitative real-world generalization.
weaknesses: Strong dependence on visible hands: The geometric calibration and cross-view transformation matrix computation (Eq. 3 and Eq. 4) strictly rely on hand visibility and reliable hand pose detection in the exocentric view. Performance drops or breakdown when hands are occluded, holding large objects, or partially out of view remain an inherent limitation.

Baseline comparisons rely on approximations: Direct codebases for key contemporaneous works such as Exo2Ego and 4Diff were unavailable, necessitating the use of proxy baselines (e.g., CFLD with ground-truth hand layout, or ablated versions of EgoWorld). While the authors' proxy setup is justifiable, a comparison with the official author numbers on identical benchmark splits would provide further clarity.

Generalization and camera setup dependency of the egocentric pose estimator: The model directly regresses 3D egocentric hand pose from a single exocentric image via a ViT-MLP regressor (phi_ego). It is not completely clear how sensitive this regressor is to arbitrary exocentric viewpoint angles and whether it requires retraining when deployed in setups with drastically different camera vantage points.

Temporal modeling remains preliminary: The current video extension mechanism relies on heuristic latent mixing (1:9 ratio), which exhibits a noticeable trade-off between image fidelity and temporal consistency.

strengths: Practical problem formulation: Translating a single exocentric image into an egocentric perspective without requiring ground-truth relative camera poses, multiple synchronized viewpoints, or a reference egocentric initial frame.

Well-motivated geometric-semantic integration: Combining metric scale calibration via hand priors, Umeyama-based coordinate transformation between predicted 3D hand poses, depth-based reprojection, and multimodal (pose + text) diffusion-based inpainting provides a principled pipeline for an ill-posed task.

Extensive experimental evaluation: Evaluated across four distinct benchmarks (H2O, TACO, Assembly101, and Ego-Exo4D) with comprehensive generalization splits covering unseen objects, actions, scenes, and subjects.

Thorough ablation and sensitivity analysis: The paper includes extensive ablations in both the main text and appendix, examining conditioning modalities, inpainting backbones (MAE, MAT, LDM), pose representations (keypoints vs. MANO), error propagation from off-the-shelf estimators, and robustness to noisy inputs.
weaknesses: High reliance on modular assembly of off-the-shelf models: The methodology primarily stitches together pre-existing foundation models (depth estimator, ACR hand pose estimator, Qwen-VL, Umeyama algorithm, and LDM inpainting), leaving the standalone machine learning contribution somewhat incremental.

Fundamental dependency on hand presence and visibility: Both the metric depth scaling (Eq. 3) and the coordinate frame transformation (Eq. 4) strictly rely on hand detection and pose estimation. In scenarios with heavy hand occlusion, manipulation of very large objects, or hands leaving the camera view, the geometric grounding stage is prone to catastrophic failure.

Substituted baselines: Direct comparisons to key modern competitors such as Exo2Ego and 4Diff are approximated via surrogate setups (CFLD and an ablated version of the proposed model) due to code availability issues, which somewhat weakens the comparative claims against exact state-of-the-art implementations.

Extension to video and temporal consistency: Although an initial video extension is discussed in the appendix, the core model remains image-based, which limits its immediate utility for continuous video translation where temporal flickering and hand-motion coherence across time are crucial.
